job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in artificial intelligence, so my day is half lectures and half training small models for my project, which sorts hospital referral letters. I share a flat in Eastbrook with three people and a very loud kettle. Evenings I'm usually building a little app for our tenants' group, and I use AI tools for nearly everything, from debugging to drafting emails. My dad drives a taxi, and there's no money to borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's stop arguing about it and get on with real problems. I'd tell my course mates that the useful bits stay useful, like drafting and debugging, and the grand promises don't happen. I'd still want rules for the tools, though, because even small automation lands on someone's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, plateau is the easy world and I'm still anxious. My degree is strong, but I owe a huge loan, I have two weeks of rent saved and openings near Eastbrook are few. A lot of the entry jobs in my field are exactly the routine tasks AI already trims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and publish the referral-sorting project, send fifty applications and keep building small apps for money. I did a landing page for a bakery for two hundred pounds last month. I'd also keep testing new tools every week, because it's how I stay ahead of other applicants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. Not scared of the world, but tired of being broke. I'd feel better with one pay cheque that wasn't a gig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. Would a plateau change how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, which I'd say I'd hardly notice, and the monthly train ticket home to see my dad. After that, the streaming and the coffees. I'd keep the broadband, because the whole side hustle runs on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut if the loan payment went up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's what I use all day already, so a plateau would just mean I keep using it. What changes is the pay. If everyone can do the basics, being good at the tools doesn't make me special.

say: I'd say the useful tools stay useful and the **grand promises** don't happen.
I'd still ask for **rules**, because small automation lands on someone's job.
think: Plateau is the easy world, but my **loan** and thin savings still worry me.
Many entry-level tasks in my field are the **routine ones** AI already trims.
do: Finish the master's and send about **50 applications**.
Keep building **small apps** for local businesses, like the bakery page.
Try one **new AI tool** every week.
feel: **Flat and tired** of being broke, but not scared of the world.
S0.quote: If everyone can do the basics, being good at the tools doesn't make me special.
fieldNote: Fluent with AI, yet still anxious because **debt** and few local jobs remain.
Already earns small sums from side projects, which shows resourcefulness.
Realises that tool skill alone is not a way to stand out.

steps.text: Send 50 applications for junior machine learning roles
Build landing pages and small apps for local shops
Test a new AI tool each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the moment for governments to write rules: a levy on firms that replace people, and money for retraining. I'd say it loudly online. I'd also say I'm tired of being told to adapt when no one is hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think entry-level coding is hit first. A senior dev with a coding assistant does the work of three juniors, and I interned at a logistics startup that stopped hiring juniors after they got one. I'm fast with the tools, but they are for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward building with AI rather than just using it, like automating workflows for small firms. I'd pick a niche, probably health admin, because of my referral project. And I'd put aside three months of rent from the app income before I commit to any one job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. I like what I can do with the tools, but I can see how thin the ladder is below me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs for people like you does Steady Disruption hit first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior developers, junior data analysts and anyone writing routine reports. Roles in customer support too. The hands-on jobs stay for longer, but I'm not a hands-on person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lean on tenants' group and union ideas. Does that fit with moving fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, in a way. I think moving fast and organising aren't opposites. I'd run an app for the tenants' group and a freelancer group at the same time, because I can build tools for the group and I get the experience.

say: I'd call for a **levy** on firms that replace people, paid into retraining.
I'd say I'm tired of hearing **adapt** when no one is hiring.
think: Entry-level coding is hit first because one senior with a tool does the work of **three juniors**.
I'm fast with the tools, but **everyone** has them now.
do: Pick a **niche** like health admin and build workflow tools for small clinics.
Save **three months** of rent from app income before committing to one job.
Start a **freelancers' group** that shares leads and rates.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**: I like what I can do, but the ladder below me is thin.
S1.quote: I think moving fast and organising aren't opposites.
fieldNote: Blends **adaptive** behaviour with progressive politics: build and organise.
Sees the squeeze on entry roles from her own internship.
Niche in health admin comes from her referral-sorting project.

steps.text: Build workflow tools for small clinics in health admin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income, a shorter working week and public ownership of the big systems, and we need them now. I'd be organising a march with the tenants' group and the freelancers. I'd also be loud that the workers building this shouldn't be the only ones who profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. If AI can do almost any thinking job by 2028, my skill is the exact thing that gets cheap, and I'd have a loan with no job to pay it. The robots come three years later, and I can't hide in a hands-on trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything except the work that earns money and pay the minimum on the loan. I'd move back in with my dad for a few months, even though the spare room is a storage cupboard. And I'd turn my app work into a small co-op with friends, so that we share clients and any basic income we get is on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also oddly alive. I'd have energy, because I like to move. I'd just be moving with a weight on my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is almost nothing. Does being good at AI tools protect you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year or two, but being good at AI tools protects me about as much as being a good typist protected clerks. I'd be early, and so would everyone like me. The edge goes when the tools can use themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth and ask if I can stay a while. He's proud of me, and he'd say not to worry, which he says about everything. I'd love for him to see me do something unusual, like a co-op, and be okay with it.

say: I'd push for a **basic income**, a shorter working week and public ownership of big systems.
I'd say the people building this should **not** be the only ones who profit.
think: If AI does thinking jobs by 2028, my skill becomes **cheap** while the loan stays.
The three-year robot gap won't help, because I'm **not a hands-on** person.
do: Pay the **minimum** on the loan and focus only on work that earns.
Move back in with my **dad** for a few months.
Turn my app work into a small **co-op** with friends.
feel: **Scared but oddly alive**, moving fast with a weight on my back.
S2.quote: Being good at AI tools protects me about as much as being a good typist protected clerks.
fieldNote: Adaptive energy keeps her **anxious** rather than alarmed, though the loan weighs.
Plans a co-op, mixing her politics with her skills.
Sees that early use of tools gives only a brief edge.

steps.text: Pay the minimum on the loan and keep earning from apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to push for a proper deal, and to see which countries get it right. I'd write about it and join the tenants' group's campaign for housing help, because housing is the thing people forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel the fear is manageable. I'd have the master's, maybe two years of work and some savings by 2031. I'd also have written the rules in my head for what I'd build, and I'd have a few clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any junior job that lets me build real systems, and keep the freelance side going on weekends. I'd put money into an index fund each month, even a small amount, so I own a bit of the thing that's replacing me. And I'd keep learning the newest tools the week they come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a dark edge. It's like running on a track with a finish line that keeps moving closer, but I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a five-year window change for you compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small firm that builds tools for clinics and councils. Four of us, one owning the sales, one the code and me doing the data. We'd earn less than a big firm, but nobody could take it from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the co-op idea look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to own something. Two years of pay would pay down the loan, and the rest goes into shares or into the firm. That feels better than waiting for a pay cheque that could vanish.

say: I'd say **five years** is long enough to push for a proper deal and see who gets it right.
I'd back the tenants' group on **housing help**, since it gets forgotten.
think: I'd have a master's, **two years of work** and some savings by 2031.
The fear is **manageable**, because I'd see it coming.
do: Take a **junior job** that builds real systems and keep freelancing on weekends.
Put a small sum in an **index fund** monthly, so I own part of what replaces me.

feel: **Hopeful** with a dark edge, like a finish line that keeps moving closer.
S3.quote: I'd put money into an index fund each month, even a small amount, so I own a bit of the thing that's replacing me.
fieldNote: The window lets her think about **ownership**, not just survival.

Co-founding a small tools firm is her answer to insecurity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the decade is a chance to build good institutions, like public data trusts and retraining that's actually free. I'd be a voice for it because people my age are the ones who'll live in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite settled. I'd have a career and the loan cleared, maybe a share in a firm. The big change comes around 2036, so I'd have time to move from using tools to owning small systems, and that's where the value will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, pay the loan down in about five years, then save for a small flat. I'd also start the firm in my late twenties and push for it to be a co-op. And I'd read policy and talk to people in other fields, because it helps to know who's affected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light, mostly. I'd still take a week in the countryside to think, because I'd be the kind of person who thinks too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still use AI tools in the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do less of the typing and more of the checking, deciding and explaining. In ten years the tools will draft nearly everything, so being the person who can say 'this is wrong' matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be true by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody is left behind, which sounds soft but isn't. I'd want a basic floor for anyone who loses work, a strong union for tech workers and my dad to retire with dignity.

I'd speak up because people my age will **live in it**.
think: I'd have a career, a cleared loan and maybe a **share in a firm** by then.
The value will be in **owning small systems**, not just using tools.

feel: **Light and settled**, though I'd still think too much.

fieldNote: With a decade she is the **calmest**, but stays uneasy about others.

steps.text: Pay the loan down in five years, then save for a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be early, but I'd have a loan, almost no savings and no time to build ownership. What would help is a basic income and a rule that firms replacing workers pay into a training fund, which I'd campaign for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss being useful in a way that someone pays for. I'd still want to build things, even if nobody paid me, but I'd want to eat too.

headlineQuote: I'd still want to build things, even if nobody paid me, but I'd want to eat too.
portrait: Kira is a **24-year-old** top computing graduate doing a master's in artificial intelligence, with a heavy loan and no family help.
She uses AI tools **every day** and earns small sums building apps for local businesses.
Her politics are progressive: she favours unions, a basic income and rules for firms that replace workers.
She moves **early**, trying co-ops, index funds and niche tools, but stays anxious about debt and entry jobs.
Only a ten-year window leaves her uneasy rather than anxious.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because she'd have debt and no time to build ownership.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and a levy on firms that replace workers, paid into free training.
